13470:
To salvage something means to save it from a situation where it was being lost, destroyed, or ruined — and to make it useful again, even if it is not perfect.

The key feeling behind the word is this: things have already gone wrong, or are going very wrong, and you step in to rescue whatever value you still can from the wreckage.
The Simplest Way to Picture It

Imagine a house is on fire. The fire has already destroyed most of it. But before everything burns completely, you rush in and pull out some furniture, some documents, some valuables. You did not save the house — it was too late for that. But you saved something from the disaster. That act of rescuing what remains from a bad situation is salvaging.

This is the heart of the word. You are not preventing a problem — the problem has already happened, or is happening. You are simply trying to recover whatever is still worth recovering.

In its most concrete sense, salvage is used when rescuing physical things from disasters like fires, floods, shipwrecks, accidents, or demolitions.

  • Workers salvaged steel beams from the collapsed building.
  • Divers salvaged gold coins from the sunken ship.
  • After the flood, she salvaged her photo albums before they were completely soaked.

Notice that in all these cases, something bad has already happened. The person doing the salvaging is working after or during the disaster, not before it.

This is where the word becomes truly powerful and widely used. You can salvage things that are not physical — like a plan, a reputation, a relationship, a deal, or even a day.

  • The chef's main dish was ruined, but she salvaged the dinner by quickly making a new sauce.
  • The team was losing badly, but a strong second half salvaged the match for them.
  • After the embarrassing mistake in the meeting, he tried to salvage his reputation by sending a thoughtful follow-up email.
  • Their friendship was nearly destroyed by the argument, but an honest conversation salvaged it.
  • The trip started terribly — flights delayed, bags lost — but a beautiful final evening salvaged the whole holiday.

In all these examples, notice the same pattern: something is going wrong or has gone wrong, and someone is trying to rescue whatever good remains.

Salvage carries a built-in sense of partial success under difficult circumstances. When you salvage something, you rarely get back everything — you get back enough. The situation was bad; you made it less bad. You could not save it all, but you saved what mattered.

This is what separates salvage from simply save. "Save" can be used in any situation — you save money, you save time, you save a file. "Salvage," however, always implies a degree of damage, loss, or failure was already present or unavoidable. You are working against the odds, recovering value from a difficult position.

Think of it this way:

  • If you catch a glass before it falls, you saved it.
  • If the glass falls and breaks, and you carefully collect the intact pieces to reuse them, you salvaged them.
The Emotional Weight of the Word

Because salvage always implies a struggle against loss or failure, it often carries a feeling of relief mixed with effort. When someone salvages something, there is a quiet heroism to it — they did not give up, they worked with what they had, and they pulled something worthwhile out of a bad situation.

This is why the word is so commonly used in emotional or dramatic contexts:

  • Salvaging a career after a big failure.
  • Salvaging a relationship after a betrayal.
  • Salvaging dignity after an embarrassing moment.
  • Salvaging a deal after negotiations nearly collapsed.

It is worth knowing that salvage implies there is something left to rescue. If a situation is completely and totally destroyed with nothing remaining, you cannot salvage it. The word only makes sense when at least some value can still be recovered. This reinforces the idea that salvage is about making the best of a bad situation — it requires that there is still a "best" to make.

To salvage is to rescue something of value from a situation that has gone wrong, is going wrong, or risks being completely lost — and to make that rescued thing useful again. It applies to physical objects and to abstract things like plans, relationships, and reputations. It always implies difficulty, partial loss, and the effort to recover what remains.
13471: A salve is something that soothes and heals. That one idea — soothing relief — is the thread running through every use of this word, whether you're talking about something physical or something emotional.

In its most concrete, physical sense, a salve is a soft, thick, creamy substance that you apply to your skin to soothe pain, heal damage, or protect an injured area. Think of the ointment a doctor might recommend for a burn, the thick balm you rub on chapped lips in winter, or the medicated cream you put on a wound to help it heal. That is a salve.

What makes something a salve — and not just any cream — is its purpose: it is specifically meant to bring relief and aid recovery. It does not sting. It does not irritate. It gently comforts and helps the skin heal.

A very common real-world example you may have already encountered is a lip salve, which is simply another name for lip balm — the small stick or pot you apply to dry, cracked lips to soothe and heal them.
The Figurative Meaning (and this is where the word gets truly interesting)

Because a salve heals physical pain, people began using the word as a metaphor — to describe anything that eases emotional or psychological pain the way an ointment eases physical pain.

So in this figurative sense, a salve is something that comforts, reassures, or reduces feelings of guilt, distress, hurt, or discomfort in the mind or heart.

Here are some clear examples to make this concrete:

"The therapist's kind words were a salve to her grief."

This means her grief felt soothed and eased by those words, the way a wound feels better after ointment is applied.

"Donating to charity was a salve to his conscience."

He felt guilty about something, and donating money soothed that guilt — it made him feel a little better about himself. The charity didn't erase what he did wrong, but it eased the sting of his guilt.

"Winning the award was a salve to her wounded pride."

She had been humiliated or embarrassed, and the award provided comfort and restored some of her self-worth.
A Very Important Nuance: Salve Soothes, But Doesn't Always Cure

This is a subtle but important detail. Whether physical or figurative, a salve relieves and comforts — but it doesn't necessarily fix the root problem completely. It takes the edge off. It makes something bearable. A salve on a wound helps it heal, but it doesn't make the wound disappear instantly. A salve to someone's conscience might make them feel less guilty, but the wrong they did is still real.

This is why the word sometimes carries a slightly skeptical tone when used figuratively. If someone says "That apology was just a salve to his guilt, not a genuine attempt to make things right," they mean the apology was more about making himself feel better than truly fixing the harm he caused.

So depending on context, calling something a salve can be either:

  • Genuinely positive — "Her hug was a salve to my sadness." (It truly helped and comforted.)
  • Slightly critical — "The government's small policy change was just a salve, not a real solution." (It gave the feeling of relief without actually solving anything deep.)
The Full Picture in One Sentence

A salve is a soothing remedy — physically, it's a healing ointment for the skin; figuratively, it's anything that brings comfort and eases emotional pain, guilt, or distress, even if it doesn't solve the underlying problem entirely.
Quick Memorable Examples to Lock It In

ContextExample
PhysicalA medicated salve applied to a burn to reduce pain
EmotionalA friend's reassurance acting as a salve to your anxiety
Guilt-relatedAn apology serving as a salve to a troubled conscience
Pride-relatedPraise acting as a salve to someone's bruised ego

Once you understand that salve = soothing relief for something that hurts, whether skin or soul, you will recognize and use this word correctly in any situation.
13472:
A salvo is a sudden burst of many things delivered together, all at once or in very rapid succession. Think of it as "a concentrated flood of things hitting at the same moment."

The heart of the word is simultaneity — not one thing trickling in slowly, but many things arriving together in one powerful, coordinated moment.
Meaning 1 — Military (Literal): Multiple Weapons Fired at Once

In its most precise, original sense, a salvo is the simultaneous firing of multiple guns, cannons, or missiles at the same target.

Imagine a warship with twenty cannons lined up on its side. Instead of firing them one by one, the crew fires all twenty at exactly the same moment. That single, coordinated blast — all weapons going off together — is a salvo.

Salvos happen in two very different situations:

As an attack: All the weapons fire together to deliver maximum force in one concentrated moment. The goal is to overwhelm the target.

As a ceremony or tribute: A salvo of gunfire is used in military funerals and celebrations. You've likely heard of a "21-gun salute" — it involves salvos fired in honour of someone. Here, the salvo isn't violent; it's respectful.

Examples in the literal sense:

  • The warship unleashed a salvo at the approaching enemy fleet.
  • Three salvos were fired in honour of the fallen soldiers.
Meaning 2 — Figurative (Everyday Use): A Burst of Words, Actions, or Reactions

This is where salvo truly thrives in modern English, and where you'll encounter it most often. We borrow that military image — many things launched together with force — and apply it to all kinds of non-military situations.

The idea stays the same: not one thing, but many, arriving fast and hard, all at once.

Examples:

  • The politician faced a salvo of criticism after the scandal. — Many critics attacking at the same time, like a barrage.
  • The press conference opened with a salvo of tough questions. — Journalists firing question after question rapidly and forcefully.
  • The company launched a salvo of new products to overwhelm its rivals. — Many products released at once as a competitive strike.
  • His announcement was met with a salvo of applause. — A sudden, loud burst of clapping all at once.

Notice something important: a figurative salvo isn't just "a lot of something." It carries a sense of force, intensity, and coordination. It implies things are being launched with purpose — like an attack, even if friendly.

One of the most frequently used expressions built from this word is "opening salvo."

Just as a battle begins with the first burst of gunfire — the opening salvo — this phrase means the first strong, aggressive move in a conflict, debate, or competition. Crucially, it implies that more is coming — it's the beginning of a fight, not the end of one.

  • His strongly-worded letter was the opening salvo in what became a bitter legal battle.
  • The company's sudden price cut was the opening salvo in a brutal price war.
  • The senator's speech was just the opening salvo — her team had much more planned.

Whenever you see "opening salvo," picture someone firing the first shot in a war that's just getting started.
The plural of salvo is salvos or salvoes — both are correct and widely used. You'll see both forms in quality writing.
A Rare, Formal Meaning (Good to Know, Unlikely to Need)

In very old legal or formal writing, "salvo" can mean a reservation or saving clause — a stated exception that protects someone's existing rights. For example, the phrase "with a salvo of his rights" means "while keeping his rights intact." This usage is almost extinct in modern English, but now you're aware it exists if you ever stumble across it in an old document.

LiterallyMultiple weapons fired simultaneously
FigurativelyA sudden, forceful burst of many things (criticism, questions, applause, actions) delivered all at once
Opening salvoThe first aggressive move in a conflict or debate, with more expected to follow
ToneAlways intense, coordinated, and forceful — never mild or casual

The word "salvo" will always carry that essential image with it: not a single arrow, but a sky full of them, all released at the same moment.
13473: The word Samaritan carries two layers of meaning — one rooted in history, and one that has grown out of it and is now widely used in everyday life. To truly understand the word, you need both layers, because the second one cannot be fully appreciated without the first.

A Samaritan, in its most direct sense, is a person from Samaria — an ancient region located in the central part of what is today Israel and Palestine. The people who lived there had their own distinct identity, culture, and religion.

Now here is the crucial part: Samaritans and Jews deeply disliked each other. This wasn't a mild discomfort — it was a centuries-old, intense mutual hostility. Jews considered Samaritans to be religiously impure "half-breeds" — people of mixed ancestry who had corrupted the true faith. Samaritans, for their part, resented Jews right back. The two groups avoided each other, refused to interact, and looked down on one another.

This tension is not just background noise. It is the key to understanding the word's second, more powerful meaning.

A small community of Samaritans still exists today — just a few hundred people living in Israel and the Palestinian territories — making them one of the oldest and smallest religious communities in the world.

In modern everyday language, a Samaritan (or more commonly, a Good Samaritan) means a person who selflessly helps someone in need, especially a complete stranger, without expecting anything in return.

When someone stops to help a stranger whose car has broken down on a highway, or when a passerby jumps into action to help an injured person on the street, we call them a "Good Samaritan." The word carries warmth — it describes someone compassionate, generous, and decent.

This meaning is so widely accepted that it now exists entirely on its own. You don't need to know anything about ancient history to use it. If someone says, "A Good Samaritan helped me when I fainted on the subway," everyone understands exactly what that means.
The Bridge Between the Two Meanings: The Parable

The reason a word for a historical ethnic group came to mean "a kind and helpful person" is one of the most famous stories ever told — the Parable of the Good Samaritan, from the Bible (Luke 10:25–37).

Here is the story in plain terms:

A man is travelling on a road when he is attacked by robbers. They beat him, strip him of his belongings, and leave him half-dead on the side of the road.

  • First, a priest walks by. He sees the wounded man — and crosses to the other side of the road to avoid him. He does nothing.
  • Next, a Levite (a respected religious figure) walks by. He too sees the man — and also passes by without helping.
  • Then, a Samaritan comes along.

Remember — a Samaritan was the kind of person that Jews of the time would have considered the last person worthy of respect. And yet, it is the Samaritan who stops. He tends to the man's wounds, lifts him onto his own animal, takes him to an inn, pays for his care, and even promises to return and pay any additional costs.

The point of the story is deliberately shocking and powerful: the person from the group everyone despised turned out to be the most truly good and compassionate of all. The "respectable" people walked past. The "wrong kind" of person showed real humanity.

This story is why the word "Samaritan" permanently bonded itself to the idea of genuine, selfless kindness toward a stranger.
How the Word Is Used Today

1. "A Good Samaritan"
The most common modern use. It describes any person who steps in to help someone — especially a stranger — in a moment of need or crisis. It has nothing to do with religion or history in everyday speech. It is simply a compliment for a kind, helpful person.

"A Good Samaritan found her wallet and returned it with every coin still inside."

2. "Good Samaritan Laws"
Many countries and states have laws called Good Samaritan laws. These are legal protections for people who voluntarily help someone in an emergency. The concern was that people might hesitate to help (for example, performing CPR on a stranger) because they feared being sued if something went wrong. Good Samaritan laws protect these helpers from legal liability, encouraging people to act.

3. "The Samaritans" (the charity)
In the United Kingdom and Ireland, The Samaritans is a well-known charitable organisation that provides emotional support to people who are struggling, in distress, or having thoughts of suicide. They offer a free, confidential listening service — anyone can call at any hour. The name was deliberately chosen to reflect the spirit of the parable: reaching out to help a stranger in their darkest moment, with no judgment.

ContextWhat "Samaritan" Means

If you see the word Samaritan in a historical or religious context, it refers to the ancient people of Samaria with their distinct identity and strained relationship with Jews.

If you see it in everyday conversation, news, or law — especially paired with "Good" — it means a kind-hearted stranger who helps someone in need, asking for nothing in return.

The deeper beauty of the word is this: it was originally the name of a group of people who were looked down upon, and yet through one story of pure compassion, it became one of the most admired things you can call a person.
13474:
To sanctify something means to make it holy, pure, or set apart for a sacred and special purpose. Think of it as a kind of transformation — something ordinary, impure, or everyday is taken and elevated into something considered clean, sacred, or morally right and legitimate.

The word always carries the idea of an authoritative act — by God, a religious figure, or even society itself — that changes the status of a person, object, place, or idea. Before sanctification, the thing is ordinary or impure. After sanctification, it belongs to a higher, holier world.

1. To make something holy and set it apart (the primary religious meaning)

This is the most direct use. When you sanctify something, you officially declare it holy and dedicate it to God or a divine purpose, separating it from ordinary everyday use.

A priest sanctifies an altar before it is used for worship. In the Bible, God sanctifies the seventh day (the Sabbath), setting it apart as a holy day of rest. A church building is sanctified before being used as a place of prayer.

The key idea is separation from the ordinary. A sanctified object or place is no longer just a thing — it now belongs to the sacred world and is to be treated with reverence.

2. To free a person from sin and make them spiritually pure

In Christian theology especially, sanctify carries a deep personal meaning. To sanctify a person is to cleanse them of sin and moral impurity, making them holy in God's eyes. This isn't usually thought of as a single moment but rather a continuous, lifelong process — a believer gradually becoming more pure, more righteous, more aligned with God's character.

This process has its own noun form: sanctification. "God sanctifies his people through truth and grace." "The Holy Spirit sanctifies believers throughout their lives." This meaning is central to Christian theology and appears heavily in the Bible and theological writing.

3. To make something morally acceptable or give it legitimacy

Beyond religion, sanctify is also used in a broader sense: to make something seem right, approved, or acceptable — often by giving it the authority of tradition, law, religion, or a moral standard.

When something is "sanctified" in this sense, it has received a kind of official blessing that makes it socially or morally valid. A wedding ceremony, for example, sanctifies a union between two people — it gives that relationship both legal standing and, in religious contexts, divine approval. Similarly: "For centuries, tradition sanctified the exclusion of women from public life — but that did not make it right." Here, "sanctified" means tradition gave it a false sense of legitimacy.

A famous related idea is the phrase "the end sanctifies the means." This means: if your goal is good enough, then any method you use to achieve it becomes acceptable. This is a morally controversial idea that many philosophers and ethicists strongly reject, but the phrase itself perfectly illustrates this third meaning of sanctify — making an action seem morally right and approved.

4. To formally dedicate something to a sacred or noble purpose

Closely related to the first meaning, to sanctify can also mean to solemnly set something apart for a special, protected purpose — shielding it from ordinary or disrespectful use.

"The battlefield was sanctified as a memorial ground, never to be built upon." "She felt her years of suffering had been sanctified by the good they eventually brought into the world." In this last example, she means her suffering was given a deeper meaning and dignity — elevated from something merely painful into something noble and purposeful.
The Thread That Runs Through All Meanings

No matter which meaning is being used, the core idea is always the same: elevation and transformation. Something moves from a lower, ordinary, or impure state to a higher, holier, more legitimate, or more dignified one. And that transformation always happens through an act of authority — divine, religious, social, or moral. You cannot sanctify something on a whim. There must be a source of authority doing the sanctifying.
How and Where It Is Typically Used

Sanctify is most at home in religious writing, theology, formal ceremonies, philosophy, and literary or historical contexts. It is not casual conversation language — you would not say "I sanctified my breakfast." You will encounter it most in the Bible and religious texts, in sermons and theological works, in ethical and philosophical discussions about what makes actions right or wrong, and in formal or ceremonial language about places, institutions, or events being consecrated or honored.

Knowing the related forms of the word makes it much more useful when you encounter it in reading.

Sanctified is the adjective and past tense form: something that has already been made holy. "Sanctified ground." "Their marriage was sanctified in the church."

Sanctification is the noun: the process or state of becoming holy or pure. In theology, sanctification is a major concept — the ongoing spiritual journey of a believer becoming more Christlike. "Sanctification is a lifelong process, not a single event."

Sanctifying is the present participle, used to describe something in the act of making holy, or something that causes holiness. "A sanctifying experience" means an experience that purifies or elevates you.

Sanctifier is a noun for the one who sanctifies — most commonly used as a title for the Holy Spirit in Christian theology.
Synonyms and Opposites (to sharpen your understanding)

Words that overlap with sanctify: consecrate (make something officially holy and dedicated — perhaps the closest synonym), hallow (honor as holy — as in "hallowed ground"), bless (invoke divine favor), purify (make clean and free of impurity), dedicate (set apart for a specific purpose).

Words that mean the opposite: desecrate (violate or damage something holy), profane (treat something sacred with disrespect or contempt), defile (make something impure or polluted), corrupt (degrade from a pure state).

Understanding the opposites is particularly helpful here — if to desecrate a place is to violate its holiness and drag it down, then to sanctify a place is to lift it up into holiness. They are mirror images of each other.
One-Line Summary to Carry With You

To sanctify = to make holy, pure, or morally/officially legitimate — elevating something from an ordinary, sinful, or uncertain state into one that is sacred, clean, or formally approved by a recognized authority.
13475:
Sanctimonious describes a person who acts as though they are morally better than everyone else — and makes sure everyone around them knows it. It is not just about having high moral standards. It is about showing off those standards in a way that is preachy, self-righteous, and often deeply annoying to others.

Think of it this way: a truly good, moral person quietly lives by their values. A sanctimonious person waves their values in your face.
Breaking It Down: The Three Key Ingredients

To call someone sanctimonious, three things are usually happening at once:

1. They believe they are morally superior.
They genuinely think they are a better, more virtuous, more righteous person than you — or at least, they act that way.

2. They make it very obvious.
This is not a private feeling. They lecture you. They look down on you. They sigh heavily at your choices. They remind you, directly or indirectly, that they would never do what you just did.

3. There is a strong hint of insincerity or hypocrisy.
This is the sharpest edge of the word. A sanctimonious person's morality often feels like a performance — something they put on to look good, not something they truly live. Very often, they quietly do the very things they criticize in others. This gap between what they preach and what they practice is at the heart of what makes the word so cutting.

Imagine you are eating a burger. Your friend looks at your plate, sighs loudly, and says:

"I just could never bring myself to eat meat. I care too much about animals and the environment. It's just a personal choice I've made because I have a conscience."

They did not need to say any of that. You did not ask. But they said it anyway — not to inform you, but to position themselves above you morally. That is sanctimonious behavior.

Now here is the twist: later, you find out this same friend secretly eats meat when no one is watching. That hypocrisy? That is the full, classic picture of sanctimonious.
The Feeling It Creates in Others

When someone is being sanctimonious toward you, you do not feel inspired or motivated to be better. You feel:

  • Talked down to, as if you are a child being lectured.
  • Judged, even when you did not ask for anyone's opinion.
  • Irritated, because the preaching feels hollow and self-serving.
  • Suspicious, because their righteousness often feels performed rather than real.

This is an important distinction. A good mentor or an honest friend might point out your flaws — and you might feel grateful for it. A sanctimonious person does the same thing, but you walk away feeling worse, not better, because their goal was never truly to help you. Their goal was to feel superior.
The Hypocrisy Angle — Why It Matters

The word carries a very strong implication that the person's moral posturing is not entirely genuine. In other words:

  • They preach honesty but bend the truth when it benefits them.
  • They preach kindness but are privately unkind.
  • They preach humility but are visibly proud of how humble they appear.

This is why sanctimonious is considered one of the more damning words you can use to describe a person's moral character. It does not say they are evil. It says something arguably worse — that they pretend to be good, that their goodness is a costume they wear for an audience.
How It Differs From Similar Ideas

It helps to understand what sanctimonious is not, so you can see its exact boundaries:

  • A strict person has firm rules and follows them. They may be harsh, but they are not necessarily sanctimonious — they may not judge others at all.
  • A preachy person lectures you repeatedly about their views. They are close to sanctimonious, but preachy focuses more on the repetition of lecturing, not necessarily the moral superiority.
  • A hypocrite does not practice what they preach. That is one element of sanctimonious, but a hypocrite is not automatically sanctimonious — they may not lecture anyone.
  • A self-righteous person is almost a synonym — they too believe firmly in their own righteousness. Sanctimonious adds the extra layer of performance and insincerity on top of self-righteousness.

Sanctimonious, at its fullest, is the combination: self-righteousness + public performance + a hollow or hypocritical core.

Not every use of the word requires full-blown hypocrisy. Sometimes, people use sanctimonious simply to describe someone who is excessively preachy and self-righteous — even if that person truly believes what they say. The core offense is still the same: they make their moral superiority known in a way that feels condescending, unsolicited, and deeply irritating. The hypocrisy deepens the insult, but it is not always required for the word to apply.

The word is used very broadly. People who get labeled sanctimonious include:

  • Politicians who moralize in speeches but live contradictory private lives.
  • Public figures who lecture their audience about values they do not personally uphold.
  • Colleagues who constantly remind you of how ethical they are in the workplace.
  • Acquaintances who make every conversation a quiet referendum on your life choices.
  • Institutions, organizations, or media outlets that adopt a tone of moral superiority while failing to live by the standards they promote.
How to Use It in a Sentence

• "His sanctimonious lecture about healthy eating felt rich, coming from someone who smokes a pack a day."
  • "She gave a sanctimonious speech about honesty, though everyone in the room knew she had lied on her résumé."
  • "I appreciate good advice, but his sanctimonious tone made it impossible to take seriously."
  • "The magazine's sanctimonious coverage of other people's scandals became embarrassing when its own editor faced similar allegations."

If you ever need to recall this word quickly: sanctimonious means acting morally superior in a preachy, self-righteous, and often hypocritical way that comes across as a performance rather than genuine virtue.

When you call someone sanctimonious, you are not complimenting their high standards. You are exposing the hollow, self-serving nature of the way they display those standards. It is a word with a sharp edge, and it lands hard — which is precisely why it is so useful.
13476:
Sanctimony is the act of performing moral goodness rather than actually living it — while simultaneously making others feel inferior for not being as "good" as you.

A sanctimonious person doesn't just believe they are morally right. They announce it, display it, and use it as a weapon to look down on others. It is self-righteousness worn like a badge — loudly, repeatedly, and usually with a tone of superiority.

Think of it this way: a truly good person does the right thing quietly. A sanctimonious person does the right thing and then makes sure everyone knows about it, often while sighing at those who don't.
Breaking It Down Into Its Two Core Parts

Sanctimony has two layers working together, and you need to understand both:

1. The Claim of Moral Superiority
This is when someone positions themselves as more virtuous, more ethical, or more righteous than the people around them. They act as though they have found the moral high ground, moved in, and built a mansion there.

2. The Insincerity or Hypocrisy Behind It
Sanctimony almost always has a hollow core. The person performing great virtue is rarely as virtuous as they pretend. They preach kindness but gossip. They lecture about honesty but bend the truth. They champion a cause publicly but privately couldn't care less. This gap between what they project and what they are is the very heart of sanctimony.

Even in rarer cases where the person isn't being hypocritical in the strictest sense, the manner in which they express their goodness — with condescension and a need to be seen — is itself considered sanctimonious.
What It Looks and Sounds Like in Real Life

Here are a few everyday examples to make it concrete:

  • A person who starts eating healthily and then lectures their friends at every meal about how terrible their food choices are, saying things like "I just care too much about my body to eat that."
  • Someone who donates to charity and then finds a way to bring it up in every conversation, making those who haven't donated feel guilty or lesser.
  • A colleague who sends an email reminding the team about environmental responsibility, while printing dozens of unnecessary pages at the office every single day.
  • A social media user who posts passionately about kindness and empathy, but responds to anyone who disagrees with them with contempt and ridicule.

Notice something in all of these: the person's goal is not just to be good — it is to be seen as good, and to make others feel not as good.
The Feeling It Creates in Others

Sanctimony has a very recognizable effect on the people around it. When someone is being sanctimonious toward you, you feel:

  • Judged — as if you are constantly being evaluated and found lacking.
  • Lectured — as if you are a student receiving a moral lesson you never asked for.
  • Embarrassed or shamed — your choices, lifestyle, or values are being held up against their "superior" ones.
  • Irritated or annoyed — because something about the performance feels fake, even if you can't immediately put your finger on why.

That last feeling — the irritation — is actually your instinct detecting the insincerity underneath the display of virtue. People who are genuinely good rarely make others feel small. Sanctimony always does.
The Key Distinction: Righteousness vs. Sanctimony

This is an important line to understand, because they can look similar on the surface.

Genuine righteousness is when a person truly lives by strong moral values. If they speak up about those values, they do so with humility, and their actions consistently back up their words. They are not trying to look good — they are trying to do good.

Sanctimony is when the appearance of virtue matters more than virtue itself. The goal — consciously or not — is to feel superior, to receive admiration, or to make others feel inferior.

A genuinely good person says: "I try to do the right thing."
A sanctimonious person says: "I can't believe you don't do the right thing. I always do."

• Sanctimonious (adjective) — the describing form. "He gave a sanctimonious speech about honesty."
  • Self-righteous — a very close synonym. Someone who is self-righteous has an exaggerated, unjustified confidence in their own moral goodness.
  • Pious — can mean genuinely devout, but when used negatively ("holier-than-thou"), it overlaps with sanctimony.
  • Hypocrite — a person who says one thing and does another. Closely linked to sanctimony, though not identical. All sanctimonious people tend toward hypocrisy, but a hypocrite isn't always being sanctimonious.
  • Smug — a related feeling of self-satisfaction. Smugness is the internal feeling; sanctimony is what it looks like when expressed outward.

If you ever want to quickly remember this word, hold onto this:

Sanctimony is the loud, insincere performance of being a good person, used to feel — and appear — morally better than everyone else.

Every time you meet someone who makes you think "they're not actually kind — they just want to seem kind, and they want me to feel bad about myself in comparison" — that is sanctimony in action.
13477: Sanction is one of the most fascinating — and tricky — words in English, because it carries two meanings that are almost direct opposites of each other. This is rare for any word, and it's the single most important thing to understand about "sanction." Once you grasp both sides, the word will never confuse you again.

In this sense, a "sanction" is an official, formal stamp of approval given by someone in authority. When a person, body, or institution with power declares that something is allowed, permitted, or endorsed — that act of approval is a sanction.

Think of it this way: imagine a sports athlete who wants to use a new piece of equipment in competition. If the governing body of that sport officially says, "Yes, this is allowed," then the athlete has received the sanction of the governing body. The sanction here is the green light from authority.

A few more examples in everyday sentences:

"The construction could not begin without the sanction of the city council." (= the council's official permission)

"She acted with the full sanction of her superiors." (= with their full, official blessing and backing)

This meaning is most common in formal writing, law, and institutional contexts. When you see "sanction" used in the singular and in a positive framing, it almost always carries this meaning of approval.

This is the meaning most people encounter today, especially in news about international affairs. Here, a "sanction" (very often used in the plural: "sanctions") is a punitive measure — a consequence deliberately imposed on someone to punish them for bad behavior and pressure them into changing course.

Think of it this way: if a student keeps breaking school rules, the school might impose sanctions — perhaps banning them from extracurricular activities or privileges. The school is using punishment as a lever to change behavior.

On a global scale, this is exactly what happens between nations. If a country violates international law or human rights, other countries or international bodies (like the United Nations) may impose economic sanctions — such as banning trade, freezing the country's financial assets abroad, or refusing to do business with them. The goal is always the same: to hurt the offending party enough that they feel compelled to change their conduct.

A few more examples in everyday sentences:

"The United Nations imposed sanctions on the regime after it ignored the ceasefire." (= punitive economic and political measures)

"The bank faced heavy sanctions for its illegal practices." (= serious penalties imposed by regulators)

"The athlete received a sanction for doping." (= a formal punishment, such as a ban or fine)
Why Does One Word Mean Two Opposite Things?

This is a completely fair thing to wonder. "Sanction" belongs to a rare class of words called contronyms (also called auto-antonyms) — words that are their own antonyms. Other examples include "cleave" (to split apart OR to stick together) and "dust" (to add dust OR to remove dust). These words developed their dual meanings over centuries as usage shifted and evolved in different directions simultaneously.

The logic connecting the two meanings of "sanction" is actually coherent if you trace it: both meanings relate to a formal, authoritative act. An authority can formally approve something (sanction as permission), or an authority can formally punish something (sanction as penalty). The common thread is that both involve an official, deliberate decision by a body that has power. Over time, each usage grew independently, and today both remain fully standard.
How to Tell Which Meaning Is Meant

Context almost always makes it clear. Here are some reliable signals:

When "sanction" means approval, you'll typically see it with words like "give," "receive," "grant," "with the sanction of," or "under the sanction of." It appears in the singular. The surrounding context feels positive or neutral — someone is getting permission to do something.

When "sanction" means penalty, it typically appears in the plural — "sanctions." You'll see it with verbs like "impose," "lift," "face," "apply," or "enforce." The context almost always involves punishment, pressure, wrongdoing, or consequences. This is the dominant meaning in journalism, international relations, and legal reporting.

If you read: "The company acted under the sanction of the board" → approval.
If you read: "The company faced sanctions from the regulator" → punishment.
One Final Thing to Lock It In

A helpful mental image: picture a judge. A judge can do two things — authorize something by signing off on it, or penalize someone by handing down a sentence. "Sanction" sits exactly at that intersection of authority. It is always an act of formal power; the only question is whether that power is being used to permit or to punish.

That's the whole word — completely and precisely.
13478: "Sanction" is one of the most remarkable — and genuinely tricky — words in English. Here is why: as a verb, it has two meanings that are almost exact opposites of each other. This is not a mistake or an accident. Both meanings are correct, both are widely used, and knowing only one of them will regularly lead you to misunderstand what you are reading or hearing. So let's cover both fully.
Meaning 1: To officially approve or authorize something

When you sanction something in this sense, you are giving it your formal, official seal of approval. You are saying, as an authority: "This is permitted. I authorize this."

The critical word here is officially. This is not casual permission from a friend. It implies that someone with real authority — a government, a board, a committee, an institution — has formally approved something.

"The government sanctioned the new medical treatment." This means the government officially approved and authorized the treatment to be used.

"The board sanctioned the merger." The board formally approved it.

"The league sanctioned the tournament." The league gave it its official authorization.

Notice that in every case, an authority is granting something — giving the green light.
Meaning 2: To penalize or punish someone for breaking a rule

In this sense, to sanction someone or something means to impose a formal punishment or penalty on them, typically because they have broken a rule, violated a law, or crossed an agreed boundary.

"The United Nations sanctioned the country for its aggression." The UN imposed penalties — such as trade restrictions or travel bans — on that country.

"The athlete was sanctioned for doping." The athlete was formally punished for using banned substances.

"The financial regulator sanctioned the bank." The regulator imposed a formal penalty on the bank.

This usage is extremely common in international politics, sports governance, and regulatory law.
How can one word mean two opposite things?

This is the most important thing to understand, and it actually makes perfect sense once you see the logic.

Both meanings are about the same thing: a formal act of authority. The difference is only in the direction of that act.

An authority can exercise its power in two ways. It can look at something and say, "Yes — this is allowed, we approve it." Or it can look at a violation and say, "No — you broke the rules, and here is your punishment." Sanction covers both of these official acts. It is the word for what an authority does, whether that is granting approval or delivering consequences.

Words that carry two opposite meanings like this are called contronyms (sometimes called auto-antonyms or Janus words). "Sanction" is the most famous example of this in the English language, and it genuinely confuses even native speakers.
How to tell which meaning is being used

Context is your only tool here, but it is a reliable one.

If a thing — a plan, an event, an action, a treatment — is being sanctioned, the meaning is almost always Meaning 1 (approved). The thing has been given the green light by an authority. Ask yourself: is this about permission being granted? Then it is Meaning 1.

If a person, company, or country is being sanctioned — especially after doing something wrong — the meaning is almost always Meaning 2 (penalized). Ask yourself: is someone being punished for breaking a rule? Then it is Meaning 2.

The word "by" is a useful signal too. "Sanctioned by the government" can go either way depending on what came before, so you always need the full sentence. For example: "The new drug was sanctioned by the government" = approved. "The company was sanctioned by the government for fraud" = punished.

A few more examples side by side to make this instinctive:

"The city council sanctioned the protest march." → The council officially permitted the march. (Meaning 1)

"The city council sanctioned the organizers for holding an illegal rally." → The council formally punished the organizers. (Meaning 2)

"The committee sanctioned the research project." → The committee approved it. (Meaning 1)

"Russia was sanctioned following the invasion." → Russia was penalized. (Meaning 2)
A mental anchor for each meaning

For Meaning 1, picture a rubber stamp coming down on a document — "APPROVED." Someone in power is stamping something as legitimate and permitted.

For Meaning 2, picture a penalty card or a court ruling — consequences being formally delivered to someone who broke the rules.

Even though the two meanings seem wildly different, they carry a shared quality that you will start to feel naturally: weight and formality. You do not use "sanction" for light, informal situations. It always implies official authority, institutional power, and formal consequence — whether that consequence is a blessing or a punishment. This is what gives the word its gravity, and why it appears so often in the language of governments, international relations, courts, regulatory bodies, and sports governing organizations.

If you train your eye to first ask "is something being approved, or is someone being punished?" every time you encounter the word, you will read it correctly every single time.
13479:
Sanctity means the quality of being so deeply important, pure, or sacred that it must be treated with the highest possible respect — and must never be violated, harmed, or taken lightly.

Think of sanctity as an invisible shield of supreme importance around something. That shield says: "This is not ordinary. This is not to be touched carelessly. This matters deeply."
The Two Main Ways It Is Used

The word operates in two closely related spaces: the religious and the moral/social.

1. Religious Sanctity — Holiness and Purity

In a religious sense, sanctity refers to the quality of being holy — being pure, close to God, and spiritually untouchable.

A person can have sanctity (a saint, a holy figure whose life is free of sin and full of devotion). A place can have sanctity (a temple, a church, a mosque — somewhere set apart from the ordinary world as belonging to God). An object or ritual can have sanctity (the holy bread in Christianity, for example).

The key feeling here is that something is set apart from the ordinary and elevated to a higher, divine level.

"The sanctity of the monastery made every visitor speak in whispers."

Here, the monastery carries such spiritual holiness that people naturally feel they must behave differently inside it.

2. Moral/Social Sanctity — Sacred Importance

Outside of religion, sanctity is used to describe things that society — or a person — treats as absolutely sacred and untouchable, not because of God, but because of their deep moral, ethical, or human importance.

This is where you'll most commonly hear the word in everyday life.

"The sanctity of human life."
"The sanctity of marriage."
"The sanctity of a promise."

When someone says "the sanctity of human life," they mean that every human life holds such supreme, irreplaceable value that it must never be carelessly destroyed or disrespected. Life, in this view, is not just important — it is sacred. It sits above ordinary concerns.

When someone says "the sanctity of marriage," they mean that marriage is not just a legal contract or a social arrangement — it is something so meaningful and solemn that it deserves to be treated with total seriousness and protected fiercely.
The Emotional Weight of the Word

What makes sanctity a powerful word is that it carries emotional and moral weight that weaker words like "importance" do not. Compare:

  • "The importance of life" — factual, calm, neutral.
  • "The sanctity of life" — urgent, reverent, deeply felt.

When you use sanctity, you are not just saying something matters. You are saying it is above challenge, above compromise, and beyond ordinary treatment. You are calling for it to be protected and revered.

• It does not simply mean something is valuable. A diamond is valuable. Sanctity implies something morally or spiritually elevated — beyond price.
  • It does not mean something is merely respected. A boss may be respected. Sanctity suggests something closer to reverence — a deeper, almost worshipful regard.
  • It is not the same as popularity or legality. Something can be sanctified and unpopular. Something can be legal but still have its sanctity violated.

You will often hear sanctity used alongside the idea of it being violated or broken. This is important because the concept of sanctity only fully makes sense when you understand what it means to breach it.

"The invasion violated the sanctity of the peace agreement."
"Graffiti on the temple walls was seen as a violation of its sanctity."

To violate sanctity means to treat something sacred as though it were ordinary — to trample on something that deserved to be protected. It carries a sense of wrongdoing, of crossing a line that should never have been crossed.

Not everything has the same level of sanctity. Society tends to assign greater sanctity to things that are:

  • Irreversible (human life — once lost, it cannot be restored)
  • Universal (values shared by all or most people)
  • Foundational (things that hold civilization, relationships, or faith together)

This is why "the sanctity of life" is a phrase with enormous power — life is irreversible and universal. By contrast, someone might speak of the sanctity of a personal promise, which carries real weight but within a smaller, personal sphere.

If you had to capture sanctity in one sentence:

Sanctity is the quality of being so holy, morally elevated, or deeply important that something deserves complete reverence and must never be treated carelessly, disrespected, or harmed.

Wherever you see this word — in a religious text, a political speech, a philosophical debate, or a personal conversation — ask yourself: What is being described as untouchable here, and why does the speaker feel it must be protected above all else? The answer to that question will always be the heart of what sanctity means in that moment.
